show_statement:
This is a bullfight staged as architecture. The guard are matadors, the corps is the animal, and the field keeps arranging itself into things that enclose — arcs, spines, wrought-iron scrollwork that looks like a balcony grille someone would watch a killing from. What it's after is the specific Spanish trick of making violence look like manners: the cape is a weapon and also a very beautiful piece of cloth, and the show refuses to pick. The audio shape backs this up — it never settles into one big arc, it spikes and drops all the way through, danger arriving in short bursts rather than one build. Where it succeeds is close: a cape mid-snap, a face after the pass. Where it strains is in the props, which are gorgeous and slightly too polite, decoration standing in for the thing being decorated. The best structural moment isn't a form at all, it's the diagonal spine at 663, where most of the field is empty and the emptiness is the point.

The cap bit, and it bit in one specific direction: I lost the wide geometry. 171 and 192 both had that enormous curved lens across the 50 that made the whole corps into a single drawn object, and dropping both means the record I'm keeping under-sells how architectural this show actually was. I'm also sorry about 123 — the standing matador and the crouched one, which was the only genuinely funny frame in 25, and comedy is the first thing an archive loses. 225 goes too, the accidental double-exposure where the broadcast dissolve turned a soloist into a ghost standing in a field of ghosts; it wasn't the show's idea, it was the tape's, and I'd have kept it for exactly that reason if I had eleven slots. 291 and 288 are near-twins and I kept the uglier one on purpose. What ten frames can't hold here is duration — this show is twelve minutes long and every keeper is an instant.

keepers.reason: The only frame where a person looks back. Everything else in this show is a body doing a shape; this is a face that has just finished doing one and hasn't put the performance back on yet. Sweat, gold braid, and an expression that isn't for us. If the show is about ritual violence, this is the one image that admits somebody is actually inside it.

Eight capes at eight different points in the same phrase — this is the show's whole argument compressed. Not a unison hit but a staggered one, which reads as more dangerous because it looks like eight separate decisions. The blur is doing more work than the bodies.

The best drill idea in the show and it's mostly empty field. A single-file spine on the diagonal with two-thirds of the turf abandoned to a handful of scattered guard — the imbalance is the statement. Most corps would have filled that space and ruined it.

A body carried horizontal through a wooden scroll by five men in white shirts. Read it as a matador being borne out of the ring and it lands; read it as furniture-moving and it also lands. That ambiguity is the most honest thing the prop package does all show.

Bodies bent double into the scrollwork so you can't tell where the prop stops and the performer starts. This is what the filigree was for and the show only fully cashes it once. Kept over its cleaner twin because the clutter is the content.

A cape whipping open in front of a wall of white pants — the guard is the event and the corps is the bull's body reduced to legs. It's the closest the show gets to a real pass, and the camera being too close to see the whole thing is what makes it work.

The gold-and-black flag change is the one time the palette stops being blood and starts being money. A dense thicket of them, poles crossing, no clean line anywhere — it's the busiest frame here and it earns the noise. The show's only genuine key change, visually.

One dancer, white shirt, empty green, arms thrown out mid-turn. The show spends most of its length insisting on mass and this frame proves it didn't need to. Isolation reads louder than the full ensemble does at 192.

The scroll props scattered through the brass at full field width, so the horn line appears to be playing inside a wrought-iron garden. Beautiful and slightly too tidy — the props behave themselves here in a way they don't at 288, which is precisely why both are worth keeping.

The opening wide, with an empty upper deck above a packed lower bowl — the stadium's own honesty about attendance, preserved by accident. The arrow form pointing at nothing yet. Kept as a before, not as a picture.
